text: A newly disclosed flaw in a leading cloud provider’s DevOps MCP server exposes a growing challenge in enterprise AI security.
The AI itself isn’t compromised. The attacker changes what the AI believes it should trust.
By hiding malicious instructions inside trusted development workflows, attackers can manipulate AI review agents into exercising legitimate enterprise permissions on their behalf.
This isn’t just prompt injection. It’s a failure of enterprise trust, where the AI becomes an unintended deputy.

As AI agents gain access to critical enterprise systems, the security question is no longer whether the AI can complete the task. It is whether the AI can distinguish trusted instructions from manipulated context before it acts.
Can the AI distinguish trusted instructions from manipulated context before it acts?
Four questions before an agent reaches production

items: What identity is the agent acting as?
Does it have only the permissions it truly needs?
Can every action be continuously verified?
Can untrusted content influence privileged decisions?

text: Every AI agent is becoming a privileged enterprise identity. Govern it with the same discipline as any other privileged account.

Zenstra AI gives each agent an owner and an identity, grants access only for the action at hand, and checks every tool call against the agent’s task before it runs, so a hidden instruction in a pull request cannot turn a reviewer’s permissions into an attacker’s.
Adapted from a post by JP Mishra, Founder and CEO, Deep Algorithms.
